name: Age
title: Prophet with a message of judgment against the house of Baasha
summary: Ahuja, son of the prophet Hanani, served as a prophet during the time of the divided kingdom and delivered God's message of judgment against Baasha, king of the northern kingdom of Israel. The prophecy declared that Baasha's dynastic house would be wiped out just like Jeroboam's house, because Baasha persistently did what was evil in the Lord's sight, led Israel into idolatry, and was guilty of shedding blood against Jeroboam's family—even though he had acted as God's instrument of punishment. The message of judgment came to pass when Zimri, one of Elah's officers, killed Baasha's son Elah and destroyed his entire lineage. Ahijah's prophetic work was also recorded in writing, and the Books of Chronicles mention his chronicle as a historical source that was included in the Book of the Kings of Israel.

keyEvents.title: Prophecy against Baasha
keyEvents.description: The word of the Lord came to the prophet Age, son of Hanani, with a message of judgment against Baasha, king of Israel. Age proclaimed that because Baasha had done what was evil in the sight of the Lord and followed the sinful ways of Jeroboam, his house would be completely wiped out. Dogs would eat those of his family who died in the city, and birds under heaven would eat those who died in the open country.

keyEvents.title: Further accusation against Baasha
keyEvents.description: Through the prophet Age came a further word of judgment against Baasha: beyond having sinned by following the ways of Jeroboam and provoking the Lord to anger through idolatry, he was also held responsible for the bloodshed against the house of Jeroboam—even though in this he had served as God's instrument to carry out the earlier judgment on Jeroboam.

keyEvents.title: Fulfillment of Age's prophecy
keyEvents.description: Age's prophecy was fulfilled when Zimri, one of King Elah's officers, conspired against and killed Elah, Baasha's son, while he was getting drunk in Tirzah. Zimri then wiped out the entire house of Baasha without sparing a single male relative, in accordance with the word that the Lord had spoken through the prophet Age.

keyEvents.title: Ages chronicle as a historical source
keyEvents.description: Age's prophetic work was recorded in writing. In 2 Chronicles, 'the chronicle of Jehu son of Hanani' is mentioned as a historical source concerning the deeds of King Jehoshaphat, and it is noted that this chronicle was included in the Book of the Kings of Israel.

versions.summary: Age was a prophet in the northern kingdom of Israel who prophesied against Baasha, king of Israel. He delivered God's judgment on the house of Baasha because of his wickedness and idolatry, similar to the judgment that had fallen upon the house of Jeroboam. Age's prophecies were fulfilled when Zimri wiped out the entire family of Baasha.
versions.title: Jehoshaphat's mortal prophet
versions.reason: [major] The title 'Jehu's Fatal Prophecy' is misleading. Jehu was a prophet who prophesied against the king of Israel (the northern kingdom), not Judah. Furthermore, 'fatal' is an odd and unclear word choice. The title should reflect his role as a prophet delivering a message of judgment against the house of Baasha.; [major] According to 1 Kings 16:1 and 2 Chronicles 16:7, Jehu was the son of Hanani. Therefore, the father's name should be set to 'Hanani'.; [major] The reference to 2 Chronicles 16:1-6 concerns the war between Asa and Baasha, not Jehu's book as a historical source. Jehu's book as a source for the history of Jehoshaphat is mentioned in 2 Chronicles 20:34. For Jehu's prophecy reproduced in the books of Chronicles, see 2 Chronicles 16:7-10 (but this concerns Hanani, Jehu's father, not Jehu himself). A reference to Jehu as a historical source is found in 1 Kings 16:7 and 2 Chronicles 20:34.; [minor] The summary is good but should mention that Jehu was the son of Hanani (a well-known prophet). This provides important contextual information.; [minor] The first three events overlap significantly with each other (all concern the same prophecy in 1 Kings 16:1-4). They could have been combined or differentiated more clearly.

versions.summary: Age, son of the prophet Hanani, was a prophet during the time of the divided kingdom who delivered God's word of judgment against Baasha, king of the northern kingdom of Israel. He proclaimed that the house of Baasha would be struck by the same judgment as the house of Jeroboam, because Baasha had done what was evil in the Lord's sight and led Israel into sin through idolatry. The prophecy was fulfilled when Zimri wiped out the entire family of Baasha. Age's deeds were written down and used as a historical source in the Books of Chronicles.
versions.title: Prophet with a message of judgment against the house of Baasha
versions.reason: [minor] The summary is good, but the sentence "Ages deeds were written down and used as a historical source in the Books of Chronicles" is slightly imprecise. It is Ages' writing/book that is mentioned as a source, not necessarily his "deeds." This should be formulated more precisely.; [minor] The title "Age's double accusation against Baasha" is somewhat imprecise. Verse 7 contains a summary that the word of the Lord came to Age and can be said to repeat or reinforce the message. "Double accusation" is an acceptable interpretation, but the wording could be clarified.; [minor] Verses 2 and 7 from 1 Kings 16 are correct references, but verse 7 also includes an additional reason for judgment (that Baasha had destroyed Jeroboam's house). Including this as a separate event from the first prophecy is reasonable, but the description should reflect this aspect more clearly.; [minor] The footnote mentions that "in Norwegian Bibles the prophet's name is rendered as Age to distinguish him from King Jehu." This is correct information, but the wording could be perceived as referring to specific translations. It should be phrased more neutrally, for example, "in the Norwegian Bible tradition."; [minor] The description states that Ages' writing "was incorporated into the Book of the Kings of Israel." 2 Chronicles 20:34 says that Age's history is "recorded in the Book of the Kings of Israel." The wording should align more closely with the biblical text.

versions.summary: Ahijah, son of the prophet Hanani, was a prophet in the time of the divided kingdom who delivered God's word of judgment against Baasha, king of the northern kingdom of Israel. He proclaimed that Baasha's house would be struck by the same judgment as Jeroboam's house, because Baasha had done what was evil in the Lord's sight and led Israel into sin through idolatry. In addition, Baasha was accused of shedding blood against Jeroboam's house, even though he himself had been God's instrument in this judgment. The prophecy was fulfilled when Zimri wiped out all of Baasha's family. Ahijah's prophetic work was also written down and recorded as a historical source in the Book of Kings of Israel, as attested in the Books of Chronicles.
versions.title: Prophet with a message of judgment against the house of Baasha
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'Additional Accusation Against Baasha' is somewhat imprecise. Verse 7 is not a separate event, but rather an elaboration and summary of the prophecy from verses 1–4. The title should reflect this more accurately.; [minor] The description states that Chronicles refers to Ahijah's writing as a source concerning 'the reign of King Jehoshaphat'. This is correct (2 Chron 20:34), but it could be clarified that it is 'Jehu son of Hanani, the chronicler' who is mentioned, and that this was 'recorded in the Book of the Kings of Israel'. The wording could be made slightly clearer.; [minor] The final sentence of the summary ('Ahijah's prophetic work was also written down and recorded as a historical source in the Book of the Kings of Israel, as attested in Chronicles') is somewhat heavy and could be improved stylistically. The phrasing is similar to version 2 – it should be varied somewhat.; [minor] Verse 7 in 1 Kgs 16 could advantageously include verses 5–6 as context for the transition from Baasha's death to the elaborated prophecy, though this is not strictly necessary.

footnotes.text: The name Age (Hebrew: יֵהוּא, Jehu) means 'He is YHWH' or 'YHWH is he'. The name is shared with the more well-known Jehu, king of Israel, who later wiped out the house of Ahab. In Norwegian Bible tradition, the prophet's name is rendered as 'Age' to distinguish him from King Jehu.

Age was the son of the prophet Hanani, who himself is known for having rebuked King Asa of Judah (2 Chron 16:7-10). The fact that both father and son were prophets suggests the existence of prophetic families or traditions passed down from generation to generation.

Age's prophecies were, according to 2 Chron 20:34, written down and included in 'the Book of the Kings of Israel'. This shows that the prophets not only spoke but also kept written records that were used as historical sources within the Deuteronomistic historical tradition.

The judgment on the house of Baasha follows a pattern known from Old Testament prophecy: whoever God raises up to punish another, but who sins themselves, will be struck by similar judgment. Baasha was exalted to carry out judgment on the house of Jeroboam, but because he followed the same sinful pattern, his own house was punished in exactly the same way.

Verse 7 in 1 Kings 16 has been discussed among scholars because it seemingly repeats the prophecy from verses 1-4, but adds an extra accusation: that Baasha struck down the house of Jeroboam. Some interpret this as an additional reason for judgment—not only did Baasha follow Jeroboam's sinful ways, but he was also guilty of bloodshed, even though he served as God's instrument to fulfill the prophecy against Jeroboam.

Hanani, Age's father, rebuked King Asa of Judah because he sought help from the Arameans instead of trusting in the Lord (2 Chron 16:7-10). Hanani was thrown into prison for this. The fact that two generations of this prophetic family confronted kings with God's judgment underscores the deep roots of their prophetic calling.
